appendExercises.q: This is **Apache Spark’s own** cluster picture. Drag the names back onto it.
appendExercises.explain: The **driver program** holds the **SparkContext**, which connects to a **cluster manager** that allocates resources; Spark acquires **executors** on the worker nodes (processes that run **tasks** and keep data in a **cache**). In Databricks classic: one executor per worker, and the platform plays the cluster-manager role.

why.sc: The SparkContext lives in the driver: it schedules tasks, it does not run them.
why.cm: The cluster manager allocates resources; it runs no tasks.
why.cache1: The cache stores data; tasks are the units of computation.
why.cache2: The cache stores data; tasks are the units of computation.

appendExercises.q: Where is your `groupBy` actually computed? Tap one place.
appendExercises.explain: In **tasks** inside the **executors** on the worker nodes — one task per partition. The driver plans and schedules; the cluster manager only allocates resources.

appendExercises.q: An application starts. Tap the steps in the order the Spark docs describe them.
appendExercises.explain: The **SparkContext** connects to the **cluster manager** → Spark acquires **executors** on the nodes → sends them your code → finally sends **tasks** to the executors to run. (Apache Spark docs, “Cluster Mode Overview”.)

appendExercises.q: Cover & recall the parts of a Spark cluster.
appendExercises.explain: Driver program (SparkContext) · cluster manager · executors on worker nodes · tasks · cache.

why.bexch: BroadcastExchange copies the SMALL side to every executor — the big side is not shuffled there.
why.aqe: AQEShuffleRead READS the shuffle output; the shuffle itself is the Exchange above it.
why.bhj: The broadcast hash join avoids a shuffle of the big side.
why.filter: A filter works inside each partition — no shuffle.

appendExercises.q: A real plan from the Spark UI. Tap the operator where the **shuffle** happens.
appendExercises.explain: **Exchange** = the redistribution / shuffle boundary (here for the aggregation). Partial aggregate before it, final aggregate after it.

why.bexch: That broadcasts the small side — the join itself is the next operator.
why.exchange: That shuffle is for the aggregation, not for the join.

appendExercises.q: Which **join strategy** did Spark choose? Tap the join.
appendExercises.explain: **BroadcastHashJoin**: the small side (Range, 100,000 rows) was broadcast (**BroadcastExchange**), so the big side joined locally without a shuffle.

regions.label: Broadcast of the small side
regions.note: The small side (Range, 100,000 rows) is broadcast to every executor.

regions.label: Partial aggregate (per partition)
regions.note: Partial aggregate: per partition, BEFORE the shuffle.

regions.label: Shuffle boundary
regions.note: Exchange = the shuffle boundary: rows are redistributed by key across the network.

regions.label: Final aggregate
regions.note: Final aggregate: combines the partial results AFTER the shuffle.

appendExercises.q: Explain the plan: drag what each covered operator **does**.
appendExercises.explain: **HashAggregate (partial)** per partition → **Exchange** (shuffle by key) → **HashAggregate (final)** combining the partial sums. The **BroadcastExchange** ships the small side to every executor for the broadcast hash join.

appendExercises.q: Follow the big side of the data from the scan to the result (skip Project and AQEShuffleRead).
appendExercises.explain: Scan → Filter → BroadcastHashJoin → partial HashAggregate → **Exchange** → final HashAggregate → TakeOrderedAndProject.

why.tasks: With 2,000 tasks you would scroll forever — the summary already shows the distribution.
why.dag-link: The DAG shows the operators, not the task-time distribution.

appendExercises.q: Your join stage is slow. Tap the part of this page where you check for **skew** first.
appendExercises.explain: **Summary Metrics**: compare **median vs max** (duration, shuffle read, spill). Median 20 s and max 15 min with a huge shuffle read on the max task = a strong skew signal.

why.c-host: The host is the machine’s address; the executor column says which executor ran the task.
why.c-locality: Locality says how close the data was, not which executor ran it.

appendExercises.q: Tap the column that tells you **where each task ran**.
appendExercises.explain: **Executor ID** — here every task says **driver**: there were no separate executors (local / single-node mode: the driver also acts as the worker).

options: Single node: the driver also acts as the worker
A multi-node compute with 0 workers running Spark normally
appendExercises.q: Open as few tiles as you can: every task ran on executor **“driver”**. What kind of compute is this?
appendExercises.explain: **Single node**: no separate worker nodes, the driver also acts as the worker. Trap: a *multi-node* compute with **0 workers** cannot run distributed Spark commands at all.

why.c-swrite: Shuffle WRITE time is about producing shuffle files, not fetching them.
why.c-fetchwait: Fetch wait is time spent waiting — not the bytes fetched.

appendExercises.q: Tap the column with the bytes each task fetched from **other** executors during the shuffle.
appendExercises.explain: **Shuffle Remote Reads**. A single task with a giant shuffle read is the classic skew picture.

why.r-duration: Batch duration helps too, but “keeping up” is arrival vs processing speed.
why.r-rows: Rows per batch alone says nothing about keeping up.

appendExercises.q: Is this query **keeping up** with its source? Tap the **two** charts you compare.
appendExercises.explain: **Input Rate vs Process Rate**. Input 100k rows/s but processed 40k rows/s sustained → backlog grows. Here both ≈ 2 rows/s → it keeps up.

why.r-process: Process rate can stay flat while each batch gets slower and slower.

appendExercises.q: Input is stable, but each micro-batch takes longer every hour (10 s → 40 s → 2 min). Which chart shows it?
appendExercises.explain: **Batch Duration**. Rising durations with stable input → inspect the stateful operators: is state (numRowsTotal) growing forever? Missing/too-long watermark, unbounded keys, bad stateful join.

options: Keeping up: processing ≈ arrival, no growing backlog
Falling behind: the backlog is growing
appendExercises.q: Uncover as little as you can: what is the verdict for this query?
appendExercises.explain: Input ≈ 2 records/s and process ≈ 2 records/s, batch duration flat around 3 s → **keeping up**. Falling behind would show process rate below input rate for a sustained time.

why.fa: A is only in v0 — v1 = {B, C} does not need it.
why.fc: C is in the current snapshot: VACUUM keeps it.
why.fd: D is not part of v1.

appendExercises.q: VACUUM ran (retention passed). Now `SELECT … VERSION AS OF 1` fails. Which missing file breaks it?
appendExercises.explain: v1 = {B, C}. C is still current, but **B** was only referenced by old versions → VACUUM deleted it. Time travel is not a backup.

regions.label: Deleted by VACUUM
regions.note: Not referenced by the current snapshot (only by old versions).

regions.label: Deleted by VACUUM
regions.note: Not referenced by the current snapshot (only by old versions).

appendExercises.q: After VACUUM (retention passed): what happens to each file?
appendExercises.explain: A and B are referenced only by old versions → **deleted**. C and D are in the current snapshot {C, D} → **kept**.

why.offsets: Offsets are about the source progress; the incompatibility is in the stored state schema.
why.metadata: The query id stays; it is the state that no longer fits.

appendExercises.q: You change `groupBy("customer_id").count()` to `groupBy("country").sum("amount")` and restart from the same checkpoint. Which part no longer fits?
appendExercises.explain: **state/** — its schema (key = customer_id, value = count) is part of the checkpoint. Changing state keys or aggregations is incompatible → new checkpoint + recomputation. State schema is effectively production data.
